summary: A 1971 note by two RAND authors with some thoughts on network graphics.

eli5.summary: Some ideas about showing pictures across the network.

questions: what did rfc 94 say about rfc 86
what is a data reconfiguration service
subtitle: RAND's reaction to RFC 86: network graphics should carry richer, higher-level descriptions than simple display codes.

tldr.problem: The network graphics proposal in RFC 86 was narrow: it described point, vector and character codes for a minimal terminal and left out features that RAND's display hardware needed.
tldr.mechanism: The authors suggest broadening it with five extensions and propose a high-level standard format, with a reconfiguration service at another node translating it for minimal hosts.
tldr.outcome: It is a discussion note: it asks for hardware information to be gathered and offers an alternative approach, without a final specification.

today: RFC 94 is a February 1971 discussion note, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text does not say what became of its proposals.

sections.title: Purpose and Starting Point
sections.content:
This note by E. Harslem and J. Heafner of RAND gives initial reactions to RFC 86, which was meant as a basis for discussion and development of network graphics. RFC 86 interprets data structures to produce graphic order codes for display. The authors say this approach has proven satisfactory and favor it.

RFC 86 targets a minimal graphics terminal connected to remote computing facilities. The authors want to also cover smart programs at both ends of a connection. They first criticize the limits of RFC 86, then suggest extensions, and lastly propose an alternate approach.
sections.eli5: Someone proposed a simple way to draw pictures from far away. The authors like the basic idea but think it should be able to do more.

sections.title: Limits of the Detailed Restrictions
sections.content:
The authors say the details of RFC 86 rule out features of RAND's display hardware that they consider necessary for some applications. Examples include line type mode and intensity control, maximum symbol sizes that are too small for their large characters, symbol origins set at the centroid rather than the lower left corner of a virtual rectangle, and 7-bit ASCII being insufficient.

They also note there is nothing to position and open a graphic compare window. They suggest that gathering the display hardware descriptions and characteristics of every node comes first, and that a mechanism for collecting this information should be defined without delay so it does not hold up network graphics work.
sections.eli5: The simple drawing rules left out things like different line styles and bigger letters. So first, everyone should write down what their screens can really do.

sections.title: Five Suggested Extensions
sections.content:
The note lists five general extensions. First, the display language should cover the union of current and anticipated network graphics hardware. Second, the data structure should allow logical as well as pictorial representation of the user's problem, as in the GRAIL Project at RAND.

Third, send definitions of graphics once and then instances of their use, such as defining a resistor once and sending only a name with attributes like position, size and rotation. Fourth, partition the display structure into static and dynamic information and into named rectangular areas, so only the dynamic part is updated. Fifth, make the interpreter context-driven so its output is not limited to one set of CRT order codes and can also feed files, using cataloged descriptions called forms.
sections.eli5: Draw a picture of a resistor once, then just say, put another one here. Only redraw the part of the screen that moves, and let the same instructions also work for other uses.

sections.title: An Alternate Proposal With Reconfiguration
sections.content:
Instead of a simple standard aimed at minimal hosts, the authors propose that communication between nodes with substantial memory and computing power use a high-level macro form rich enough to express the special features of network display devices. A terminal should normally connect only to a program that addresses no more than its hardware capabilities. A simple terminal and simple program can still communicate, as in RFC 86, within the same standard.

Minimal hosts that cannot translate the powerful standard would use another network node that provides data reconfiguration services, which the authors call an essential part of the proposal. It would translate from the network standard to the specific non-standard format the minimal node needs, using a data base of forms. The note's figures show such a service and its use as an intermediary by two remote nodes.
sections.eli5: If a small computer cannot understand fancy drawing instructions, a bigger computer in the middle translates them into a simpler form it can use.

items.title: Union of hardware
items.text: Cover current and anticipated network graphics hardware.

items.title: Logical and pictorial
items.text: Represent the meaning of a picture along with the picture.

items.title: Definitions, then instances
items.text: Define a graphic once and send instances with attributes.

items.title: Partitions
items.text: Separate static from dynamic parts and use named rectangles.

items.title: Context-driven interpreter
items.text: Output is not limited to one set of CRT order codes.

references.text: The network graphics proposal this note responds to.
